video_notes.title: Build a Complete End-to-End GenAI Project in 3 Hours
video_notes.contributed: A single-person, single-repo AI news aggregator build (scrapers to database to agents to email to render deployment) that shows the moment-to-moment prompting and architectural-decision loop with a coding agent.

video_notes.title: Build a Full-Stack GenAI Project in 4 Hours (FastAPI, React, Supabase)
video_notes.contributed: A monorepo full-stack RAG build (FastAPI + React + Supabase + pgvector) for a hypothetical client, showing agents.md-driven setup, hybrid retrieval with agentic tool loops, grounding/citation validators, and a Railway deployment.

video_notes.title: How I Build and Ship Custom AI Solutions for Clients
video_notes.contributed: The agency-level process: discovery, scoping into PoC vs MVP, proposal structure, two-week sprint cadence and pricing, the standardized Genai Launchpad stack, and the Hetzner/Caddy/Langfuse/Sentry deployment and monitoring setup.

video_notes.title: How to Systematically Setup LLM Evals (Metrics, Unit Tests, LLM-as-a-Judge)
video_notes.contributed: A dedicated framework for the three levels of LLM evals (unit tests, human+LLM-judge, A/B testing), the analyze-measure-improve loop, and the human/LLM alignment process with concrete agreement-score tooling.

claims.claim: Start a new build by speech-to-texting a free-form brain dump of the idea and feeding that raw transcript into an AI tool's plan mode before writing any code.
claims.quote: I want to use some kind of speech to text tool in order to just do a brain dump

claims.theme: Be the architect, not the passenger
claims.claim: Give the AI agent specific technical constraints up front (exact DB, ORM, language, folder layout) during planning so the agent's plan reflects your architecture rather than its own default.
claims.quote: we are the architect

claims.theme: Reference docs over letting AI guess
claims.claim: When a library behaves unexpectedly (e.g. YouTube Transcript API's fetch vs get_transcript), stop and pull the quick-start docs rather than letting the agent keep guessing at the API.
claims.quote: always try and reference some kind of like quick start documentation

claims.claim: Never name a project file the same as a package you import (e.g. a file called openai.py in a module that imports the openai package) — it causes confusing import errors.
claims.quote: don't accidentally have a file name in Python that is similar to a package that you're importing

claims.claim: Before building a custom scraper, check for an RSS feed (OpenAI has one; a third party maintains unofficial feeds for sites like Anthropic that lack one) — RSS is far more reliable than scraping a JS-heavy or Cloudflare-protected page.
claims.quote: turns out there is an RSS feed for OpenAI as well

claims.claim: OpenAI's site actively blocks scraping attempts via Cloudflare, so full-page content extraction (even with Docling) fails there and you must fall back to RSS title/description only.
claims.quote: OpenAI is really tricky with scraping any information from their website

claims.claim: Separate pipelines into a fast metadata-only ingestion stage (store title/URL/ID quickly) and a slower content-processing stage (transcript/markdown extraction) that runs afterward or in background — don't block scraping on expensive extraction.
claims.quote: store metadata no transfer fast get all the items and then process

claims.claim: Data Lumina's commercial 'Genai Launchpad' is the production boilerplate used for all client builds, handling infra setup, agent definitions, and Docker — sold separately from the free YouTube content.
claims.quote: this is actually a product that we offer

claims.theme: Primary keys to dedupe scraped data
claims.claim: Use natural IDs (e.g. video ID) as database primary keys so re-running a scraper never creates duplicate rows; decide explicitly whether re-ingestion should skip or update existing rows.
claims.quote: there's no duplicate data

claims.claim: Explicitly filter out YouTube Shorts in a channel scraper — they are usually clips of longer videos and the transcript API is unreliable for them.
claims.quote: Can you actually make it so that shorts are skipped entirely?

claims.theme: Residential proxy for YouTube transcript scraping at scale
claims.claim: YouTube will temporarily IP-block high-volume use of its internal transcript API; use a rotating residential proxy service (e.g. Webshare, ~$4-5/month cheapest plan) configured on the YouTube Transcript API client to avoid blocks in production.
claims.quote: YouTube will temporarily IP block you

claims.theme: Push back on AI architecture suggestions
claims.claim: Don't blindly accept an agent-proposed schema change (e.g. a 'message_citations' table) — ask the agent to justify why the table/field is needed before approving it.
claims.quote: a little bit of a of a push back

claims.claim: If you accidentally commit a .env file before adding it to .gitignore, git rm --cached (or AI-assisted equivalent) is needed to stop tracking it without deleting the local file — gitignore alone won't untrack an already-committed file.
claims.quote: I accidentally pushed my file to GitHub

claims.claim: For personal/portfolio projects, send email via Python's smtplib with a Gmail account and an app password — no paid service or external account needed; for client/production work use a dedicated service like Resend instead.
claims.quote: Python has an SMTP lip

claims.claim: Docling loads local OCR-capable models and can exhaust memory on small cloud instances; swapping to the lighter Rust-based html-to-markdown library (lower fidelity but far less memory) fixed an out-of-memory crash on a Render deployment.
claims.quote: we were running out of memory

claims.theme: Manually create tables on first deploy
claims.claim: If a cron/scheduled job fails because tables don't exist yet on a fresh production database, add a table-existence check inside the daily runner that creates tables on first run, instead of relying solely on a deploy-time migration step.
claims.quote: we manually create them in the daily runner

claims.claim: Build an explicit ENVIRONMENT=local|production setting (not just inferring from whether a DATABASE_URL happens to contain 'render') so migrations and scripts never accidentally hit the wrong database.
claims.quote: it automatically assumes that this is the production environment

claims.theme: Refactor to base classes once duplication appears
claims.claim: Once two or more scrapers (or repository functions) share ~80% identical logic, refactor into a base class with inheritance (BaseScraper → OpenAIScraper/AnthropicScraper) rather than keep copy-pasting, and introduce a scraper registry pattern so adding a new source doesn't touch the runner.
claims.quote: the entropic scraper and the openi scraper share 80% identical RSS parsing logic

claims.claim: A freshly deployed database defaults to being publicly reachable (0.0.0.0/0 inbound); use a dedicated static IP (e.g. via an N-layer/VPN gateway) to whitelist only your team's connections at the database/firewall level.
claims.quote: right now it's set to like 00 0

claims.claim: The distinguishing feature of 'AI-assisted/agentic coding' versus 'vibe coding' is staying in control of architecture decisions while letting AI handle execution — not avoiding AI, and not blindly accepting everything it outputs.
claims.quote: this is not vibe coding, this is AI assisted coding, this is agentic coding

claims.claim: Put frontend and backend in a single mono-repo (not separate repos) when using coding agents, because the agent can reason over the full context across both layers at once.
claims.quote: This works super well when you are using coding agents because they can reason over the entire context

claims.theme: Why internal tools beat ChatGPT for enterprise
claims.claim: Enterprises reject plugging proprietary documents into off-the-shelf tools like ChatGPT/Copilot for two reasons: data privacy/compliance (needs a whitelisted endpoint via AWS Bedrock/Azure) and the need for a customization layer so 40 analysts get standardized, not generic, output.
claims.quote: it is simply just a nogo to let everyone pretty much use CHBT

claims.claim: For high-stakes document Q&A, every claim must cite the specific filing and page, and the application must treat the analyst as still responsible for fact-checking — the tool accelerates intake, it doesn't replace verification.
claims.quote: cites the specific file in a specific page

claims.claim: Maintain an agents.md file (top-level plus one per major folder like frontend/backend) that is auto-injected into every coding-agent session; for Claude Code, rename it to CLAUDE.md to get the same effect.
claims.quote: turn this into a clot.md file

claims.claim: Protect dependencies from supply-chain attacks by setting a minimum-release-age in .npmrc (pnpm) so packages younger than 7 days can't be installed, and use exact version bounds with 'exclude newer than 7 days' in pyproject.toml for Python.
claims.quote: a minimum release age so that we cannot import literally we cannot import packages that are younger than 7 days

claims.theme: Small bite-sized prompts beat giant plans
claims.claim: When you deeply understand the problem, incremental bite-sized prompts with review checkpoints are faster than one giant plan executed unattended for hours — the big-plan approach works but risks losing codebase understanding.
claims.quote: it's usually way faster to work in small inter incremental bite-size prompts

claims.claim: Special characters in a database password (#, %, backtick) can break environment-variable parsing in a connection string; wrap the DATABASE_URL in quotes in the .env file to fix it, or reset to a password without special characters.
claims.quote: use the quotes around it

claims.claim: Use pydantic-settings (BaseSettings) to load environment variables because it raises a clear validation error naming the specific missing required field, which is far easier to debug than silent failures — especially valuable during deployment.
claims.quote: we got a validation error and what there is a particular required field that is missing

claims.claim: A SQLAlchemy connection using psycopg (v3) vs psycopg2 requires rewriting the DATABASE_URL scheme (adding the driver suffix); without it you get import/connection errors that look unrelated to the actual cause.
claims.quote: if you have Psychob G without the two after it, it uses version three

claims.theme: Disable public signup for internal tools
claims.claim: For an internal-only tool built on Supabase auth, disable 'allow new users to sign up' and manually create accounts with auto-confirm — otherwise anyone who finds the deployed URL can self-register.
claims.quote: I'm going to disable allow new users to sign up

claims.theme: Keep ingestion scripts out of the app folder
claims.claim: One-time/local data-processing scripts (HTML-to-markdown conversion, manual DB seeding) that the deployed app doesn't depend on should live in a separate data/ingest folder outside the application code, as a matter of deployment hygiene.
claims.quote: keep it out of your like application folder because it's code essentially that your app doesn't rely on

claims.claim: Docling's hybrid/hierarchical chunker respects document headers and structure instead of naive fixed-token splitting, producing better chunk boundaries for RAG — but struggles with tables, which can still come out malformed.
claims.quote: it applies tokenizationaw aware refinements on top of the document based hierarchical chunking

claims.theme: Postgres full-text search needs keyword extraction
claims.claim: Feeding a user's full natural-language question directly into Postgres full-text search almost never matches; first run an LLM call to extract 3-5 meaningful keywords (and strip filler/stopwords) before the full-text query.
claims.quote: if you do a full user query there will almost never be a match

claims.claim: Instead of a naive 'retrieve once, stuff into prompt' RAG pipeline, build an agent with tools (search_filings, read_chunk, read_surrounding_chunks) so it can decide it needs more context and go back to the database — trading speed/cost for better grounding.
claims.quote: it can search filings, it can read uh chunks, it can read a chunk and it can also read surrounding chunks

claims.claim: After the agent produces an answer, run a second validator step that re-checks every citation against the actually-retrieved chunks and rejects any chunk ID that was never retrieved, forcing a hard pass/fail before returning the answer to the user.
claims.quote: rejects chunks ideas that were never retrieved

claims.theme: Keep Docling out of main dependencies
claims.claim: Docling is heavy enough that including it in main (not dev/optional) dependencies can make deployment fail on constrained compute (low RAM/CPU); keep it in an optional/dev dependency group.
claims.quote: dockling can is a quite an extensive library

claims.theme: Custom HTML table extractor beats generic parser
claims.claim: For structured source documents (SEC filings) with many tables, a dedicated custom HTML table extractor produced correctly rendered markdown tables where Docling's general-purpose conversion mangled them — worth the extra build step for citation-critical UIs.
claims.quote: it's better to just rely on HTML parsing in order to get this out

claims.claim: Running every user query (even 'hi, what can you help with') through the full agentic search pipeline wastes time and model cost; add a query-classification step to route simple/greeting/follow-up questions to a cheaper direct answer instead of the full retrieval loop.
claims.quote: query classification. So we check okay what kind of question is this?

claims.claim: Running a sophisticated multi-call agentic RAG pipeline on a frontier model (GPT-5.5) can cost roughly $1-2 per query, which must be factored into the business case before choosing model tier.
claims.quote: this can easily become like one one to two $1 probably something like that per query

claims.theme: Deployment is push code + run startup command
claims.claim: The universal mental model for deployment, regardless of platform (Render, Railway, Hetzner), is: push your code to a rented always-on server, set environment variables, and run the same startup command you used locally.
claims.quote: deploying is nothing more than pushing all that code to some kind of like cloud server

claims.theme: Don't let an MCP server hold production credentials
claims.claim: Letting a deployment MCP server (e.g. Railway's) handle API keys and infra setup directly is explicitly not how production client work is done — it's acceptable in a demo project you plan to tear down, not for real credentials.
claims.quote: this is not something that I would do on a client project

claims.theme: First version is only the beginning
claims.claim: A single purple 'phase' block that an agent appears to one-shot in a tutorial would, in a real client project, take at least a full day to properly validate (prompts, tool outputs, edge cases) — the speed of generation does not equal the speed of a production-ready result.
claims.quote: you'll spend at least a day on any one of those purple building blocks

claims.theme: Discovery call separates real ROI from hype
claims.claim: In discovery calls, actively push back on client-proposed use cases biased toward 'we think AI can do this' — dig for the simplest high-impact automation (sometimes simple n8n/Zapier integrations, no LLM needed) rather than accepting the client's framing.
claims.quote: always pick the quick wins over the moonshots

claims.claim: Red flags to screen out during discovery: motivation is only 'everyone's doing AI,' no clear success criteria exist, and the client expects 100% accuracy from day one.
claims.quote: some clients expect magic from day one

claims.claim: A first LLM-based build typically reaches 70-80% accuracy; iteration usually gets you to about 90% — clients used to deterministic software need to be explicitly educated that this is the normal curve, not a failure.
claims.quote: Your first build typically gets to 70 or 80% accuracy. After iteration, you can usually get to 90%

claims.claim: Distinguish human escalation (system routes only the ~20% of cases it can't confidently handle to a person) from human-in-the-loop (every output requires human approval before it goes live) — pick based on error-impact tolerance for the use case.
claims.quote: we identify the 80% of the tickets that we can handle and we escalate 20%

claims.theme: Proof of concept vs MVP distinction
claims.claim: Frame first client deliverables explicitly as either a Proof of Concept (local demo proving the KPI is achievable, not yet production value) or an MVP (minimum but real, deployable, value-adding product) — be upfront about which one you're billing for, since clients often assume a PoC is already usable.
claims.quote: a proof of concept is usually not something that adds value

claims.claim: A client proposal should contain, in order: problem statement in the client's own words, proposed solution with scope boundaries, technical approach, what's included/excluded, success criteria and measurement, then timeline and pricing.
claims.quote: we start with the pro the problem statement

claims.claim: Price custom AI dev work in two-week sprints at 10k-20k EUR per sprint; structure each sprint as day 1-2 architecture setup, day 3-8 core development/integration, final days testing/polish/demo.
claims.quote: we'll price that between 10k to 20k in euros per sprint

claims.theme: Always quote ongoing costs, not just build cost
claims.claim: Beginners often forget to quote ongoing infrastructure and LLM API costs alongside the upfront build price — always give a rough estimate of recurring costs in the proposal, even though exact prediction is hard.
claims.quote: beginners often forget where say like hey I am going to build this chatbot for you 5k

claims.claim: Push for async updates instead of recurring standups with clients to minimize meeting overhead; only hold a kickoff call at sprint start and a demo call at sprint end.
claims.quote: we always push for async updates. We don't want to do standups

claims.claim: Real sprint cadence is rarely back-to-back; plan for client-side delays of 2-8 weeks between sprints due to internal testing and reprioritization, and mitigate cash-flow risk by overbooking slightly with a pipeline of other clients.
claims.quote: this can take anywhere from two sometimes oh sorry sometimes even like up to eight weeks

claims.claim: Standardize every client backend on one framework (FastAPI, Celery, Postgres, Redis, self-hosted Supabase, Pydantic AI) via a forkable boilerplate repo so every project has identical folder structure, enabling fast context-switching between concurrent client projects.
claims.quote: same stack, same patterns, same deployment process every single project

claims.theme: Azure OpenAI for compliance despite friction
claims.claim: Azure OpenAI is used for most client LLM calls specifically to satisfy enterprise data-compliance requirements, despite disliking its frequently changing interface and restrictive quotas.
claims.quote: Not the happiest with it. It's kind of like annoying

claims.theme: Pull raw production events for eval tests
claims.claim: Build unit/eval tests from real raw JSON payloads pulled from the production database rather than only synthetic dummy data, so evals reflect actual failure patterns.
claims.quote: later we constantly pull raw records from the database

claims.theme: Skills built from recurring debugging tasks
claims.claim: Turn repeated support/debug workflows (pull a specific ticket from the DB, assess what went wrong) into a Claude Code skill (SKILL.md) once you catch yourself doing the same task manually more than two or three times.
claims.quote: we've been creating actual skills

claims.theme: Vanilla Claude Code, 1-3 sessions at a time
claims.claim: Run Claude Code (currently Opus 4.6) in plan-mode-then-execute with only one to three concurrent sessions on the same branch — avoid 10-agent worktree setups because they become impossible to oversee.
claims.quote: I usually like to work with one or three sessions at a time

claims.theme: Prime fresh sessions with explicit pointers
claims.claim: Every coding-agent session starts with zero codebase knowledge; prime it by naming the exact docs/files to read first, otherwise it reindexes the whole codebase and burns half the context window before useful work starts.
claims.quote: it's going to reindex your codebase and it is for itself going to think and try to search for everything

claims.claim: Client deployments run on a cheap Hetzner bare-metal VM with Docker Compose, pulled via a GitHub-Action-triggered pull-based CI/CD script, fronted by Caddy as a reverse proxy for automatic HTTPS — roughly 10x cheaper than Azure/AWS for this team's scale.
claims.quote: This is literally 10 times cheaper

claims.claim: Deploy with a default-deny firewall (only ports 80/443 open), use a dedicated static VPN IP for team and database access, and whitelist only services that need it — never leave a database reachable from any IP.
claims.quote: you want to like block everything by default and then whitelist services

claims.theme: Langfuse + Sentry as the two monitoring tools
claims.claim: Use Langfuse for LLM trace monitoring (prompt-level debugging, every workflow step automatically tracked) and Sentry for application error tracking piped to a Slack channel — together they are described as the 'two secret weapons' for production AI observability.
claims.quote: we have two secret weapons for this

claims.theme: Copy Sentry error as markdown into the agent
claims.claim: Sentry lets you copy an error event as markdown; pasting that directly into a coding agent (e.g. Claude Code) is often enough for it to diagnose and fix the bug on the spot.
claims.quote: you chug it into cloud code and it fixes fixes it on the spot

claims.theme: Keep pricing flat, use speed to increase margin
claims.claim: Rather than racing to the bottom on price as AI makes delivery faster, keep sprint pricing the same and use the extra speed to take on more client requests/features at the same cost — described as a 'golden era' before the market recalibrates.
claims.quote: we pretty much keep the pricing the same

claims.theme: One big client can hit six figures
claims.claim: A single large ongoing client contract can put a solo freelancer at the six-figure revenue mark — the long-term play is becoming a client's recurring 'AI development partner' rather than chasing many one-off projects.
claims.quote: that could like that could put you at a six-figure mark

claims.theme: Never hit a scaling ceiling on single-VM + Celery
claims.claim: The team has never needed Kubernetes across years of client projects — a single VM with Celery/Redis as a task queue scales further than most people assume before container orchestration becomes necessary.
claims.quote: we've never hit the limit of where where this kind of like breaks

claims.claim: Gartner projects 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by 2027; MIT reports 95% of generative AI pilots are failing — cited as directional evidence even if the exact numbers are uncertain.
claims.quote: by 2027, 40% of all agent AI projects is expected to be cancelled

claims.theme: Three core challenges in LLM development
claims.claim: LLM systems face three compounding challenges: not understanding what data flows through the system at scale, a gap between what you can specify in prompts/code and what 'good' looks like, and inconsistent behavior where small wording changes produce very different outputs.
claims.quote: the three core challenges in LLM development

claims.claim: Evals exist at three escalating levels: Level 1 unit tests (fast, cheap, run on every change), Level 2 human+LLM-judge evaluation (run weekly/bi-weekly, needs humans in the loop), Level 3 A/B testing (run on major releases, measures real business impact) — cost and effort increase at each level.
claims.quote: the cost and effort increase with each level

claims.claim: Apply an iterative analyze (collect/categorize failure modes) → measure (turn insights into quantitative boolean/scored metrics) → improve (refine prompts, models, architecture) cycle, borrowed from Hamel Husain and Shankar's application-centric AI evals framework.
claims.quote: analyze, measure, improve life cycle

claims.theme: Unit tests via plain Python asserts on structured output
claims.claim: Build Level 1 LLM unit tests as simple Python asserts over structured (pydantic) output fields (category in allowed set, confidence is a float between 0-1, response length > N) run against stored raw JSON events in an evals/events folder.
claims.quote: we typically put these in the the eels folder and then we have some events in there

claims.theme: LLM-as-judge must use the most powerful model
claims.claim: When moving to Level 2 LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, use the most powerful model you can afford (not cheap/mini models) and require detailed critiques explaining the reasoning, not just a bare score.
claims.quote: you uh you typically want to use the most powerful model that you can afford

claims.theme: Judge must be aligned to human judgment first
claims.claim: An LLM judge is worthless until validated against human domain-expert judgments on the same data — the process is: collect model predictions, generate model critiques, get human evaluations on the same data, compare, iterate on the judge prompt, repeat until agreement is sufficient.
claims.quote: It must be aligned with human judgment

claims.claim: Track human-vs-LLM-judge agreement in a simple spreadsheet (10-100 examples: input, output, model critique, human critique, match=1/0) and compute an agreement score (e.g. 70%) that you then iterate up by refining the judge prompt, including via meta-prompting with a powerful model.
claims.quote: there is a 70% agreement score

claims.theme: AB testing is the most expensive and trickiest eval level
claims.claim: Level 3 A/B testing (comparing prompts/models/workflows against real user outcomes like satisfaction, task completion rate, time to resolution) requires enough user volume to be worthwhile and the agency itself hasn't fully automated it yet — they still mostly do small manual prompt A/B comparisons.
claims.quote: we at data lumna we haven't even gotten to the point with our applications yet where we really have automated ab testing

claims.claim: Reference-based metrics (exact match, semantic similarity, code execution, SQL correctness) apply when you know the golden answer and are easier to automate; reference-free metrics (tone, length, hallucination, safety/toxicity) are needed when multiple valid outputs exist and require scored rubrics.
claims.quote: are reference based metrics

claims.claim: Avoid four common eval mistakes: tool-first thinking (buying a new vector DB/model/eval platform before understanding the problem), generic metrics obsession (meaningless averaged scores like 'helpfulness 4.2'), avoiding looking at your own data, and shipping an unaligned LLM judge without human validation.
claims.quote: tool first thinking

claims.theme: Engineers who look at data outperform those who don't
claims.claim: A principal engineer at Zapier reportedly spends three hours per day looking at traces and raw data — manual inspection of real data has the highest value-to-effort ratio in AI engineering and should never be skipped.
claims.quote: a principal engineer at Zapier who spends three hours per day looking at traces and data

claims.theme: Signs you're succeeding vs struggling with evals
claims.claim: You're succeeding at an evaluation-driven workflow when you can deploy changes confidently, failures are caught before users see them, and improvements compound; you're struggling when fixes break other things, you're surprised by user complaints, and progress feels like trial and error.
claims.quote: You'll know you'll succeeding when you can deploy changes confidently

disagreements.topic: How much weight to give big upfront AI agent plans vs. small incremental prompts

positions.position: Prefers small, bite-sized incremental prompts with frequent review checkpoints over letting an agent run unattended on a huge plan for an hour, to stay oriented in the codebase.
Repeatedly hands the agent large multi-step instructions (e.g. 'create the digest agent, the database model, and the processor') and lets it execute a big chunk in one go, checking in only afterward.

disagreements.topic: Whether to let AI/MCP tools handle production credentials and deployment directly

positions.position: Explicitly uses an MCP server to let the agent configure Railway and handle credentials directly, while flagging that this is not how it's done for real client projects.
Insists on manual, access-controlled deployment (block-all-by-default firewalls, dedicated static IP, private networks) for all real client work — no MCP-driven credential handling.

gaps: No corpus content on how to measure or prove the '3 hours saved per analyst per week' success metric mentioned as the RAG project's definition of done — the demo build never gets tested with real analysts.
No discussion of exact pricing or contract terms for the LLM evals program/consulting beyond the sprint pricing given in Q679gH7oszg; the eval video doesn't connect its framework back to billing.
No detail on how the agency actually recruits, interviews, or onboards subcontractors mentioned in Q679gH7oszg beyond 'depending on the contracts' — the hiring process itself is not covered.
No concrete numbers on LLM API cost for the news aggregator or document-copilot projects beyond the single qF5il_9IwME remark about $1-2 per RAG query — no monthly cost estimate for either demo app.

The videos never show what the actual LLM-as-judge prompt looked like after iteration to reach high agreement, only the general meta-prompting technique — no worked example of a 'good' judge prompt verbatim.

No coverage of how Pydantic AI's tool-calling loop actually decides when to stop calling tools versus finalize an answer (the internal stopping criteria) — only that it 'decides' based on instructions.

No discussion of multi-tenant security hardening (RLS policy specifics, rate limiting, abuse prevention) beyond enabling Supabase row-level security by default — the videos don't show what a bad RLS policy misconfiguration looks like.
